description: We’re a team from the ISAT U Space Society, a group of students passionate about space science, technology, and exploration. Our members bring together interests in astronomy, engineering, research, and creative problem-solving, and we love turning big ideas into practical solutions.
summary:
We developed a remote sensing and GIS workflow that estimates the methane emission potential of rice-growing areas in Iloilo Province. Flooded rice paddies are a known source of methane, a greenhouse gas that drives climate change, but localized data on these emissions is limited. Our approach uses Sentinel-2 optical imagery to map rice cultivation areas and Sentinel-1 radar imagery to monitor field flooding patterns, even through cloud cover. These outputs are then combined with suitable emission factors in GIS to produce rice distribution maps, inundation maps, and estimated methane emission potential maps that highlight priority areas.

This addresses the challenge by turning free, open satellite data into area-specific information that would otherwise require costly field measurements. It also pairs the findings with practical mitigation measures: Alternate Wetting and Drying, better irrigation scheduling, residue management, and farmer education.

It matters because it helps local agencies and farmers target climate action where it will have the most impact, supporting sustainable rice farming while protecting food production.
details:
What it does and how it works

Our project uses satellite imagery and GIS to estimate how much methane flooded rice fields in Iloilo Province may release. Flooded paddies create oxygen-poor soil conditions where microbes produce methane, a greenhouse gas that contributes to climate change. Localized data on this is limited, so we built a workflow that answers four questions: how much rice area exists, how the fields are flooded over time, which areas have the highest estimated emission potential, and what mitigation strategies can reduce emissions.

The workflow has four stages:

  1. Map rice farms with Sentinel-2. Optical imagery is used to identify and delineate rice cultivation areas.
  2. Monitor inundation with Sentinel-1. Radar imagery detects standing water in fields, even through cloud cover, which is common in the Philippines during the rainy season.
  3. Estimate methane with GIS and emission factors. Rice area and flooding patterns are combined with suitable emission factors to estimate methane emission potential per area.
  4. Produce results. The outputs are a rice farm distribution map, field inundation maps, estimated methane emission potential maps, and recommended mitigation measures.

Benefits

  • Localized information. It fills the gap in area-specific methane data for Iloilo’s rice farms.
  • Cost-effective and scalable. Sentinel data is freely available, so the method can be repeated across seasons or extended to other provinces.
  • Cloud-independent monitoring. Radar data keeps flood monitoring reliable year-round.
  • Targeted action. Priority areas are identified, so limited resources go where emission potential is highest.

Intended impact

The study aims to identify rice-growing areas with higher estimated methane emission potential and to support climate action through improved water management and sustainable rice farming. Our proposed mitigation measures are:

  • Alternate Wetting and Drying (AWD): reduce continuous flooding where feasible.
  • Improved water management: better irrigation scheduling.
  • Residue management: proper handling of rice straw and organic materials.
  • Farmer education: promoting climate-smart farming practices.

The results can help local government units, agricultural agencies, and farmers make evidence-based decisions that reduce emissions without sacrificing rice production.

Tools and technologies

  • Satellite data: Sentinel-2 (optical) and Sentinel-1 (SAR/radar) from the Copernicus program
  • GIS software: for spatial analysis, map production, and combining emission factors with mapped areas
  • Emission factors: standard factors (e.g., IPCC-based) adapted to local water regimes

Creativity

The project’s creativity lies in combining two complementary satellite sensors, optical for where rice is grown and radar for when and how long it is flooded, to estimate a gas that can’t be seen directly. Instead of expensive field gas-sampling equipment, we infer emission potential from observable flooding behavior. It also links the science directly to practical solutions, going from detection to mapping to mitigation recommendations.

Factors our team considered

  • Data availability and cost: using open-access satellite data
  • Cloud cover: choosing Sentinel-1 radar for dependable flood monitoring
  • Water management practice: since flooding duration drives methane production
  • Choice of emission factors: selecting ones suited to local conditions
  • Feasibility for farmers: recommending mitigation like AWD only “where feasible,” so food production and livelihoods are protected
  • Limitations: the results are estimates of potential, not direct measurements, and would benefit from field validation
